newsitem.title: USA: Dollar ends higher in guarded U.S. dealings.
newsitem.headline: Dollar ends higher in guarded U.S. dealings.

text.p: *Dollar closed firmer vs mark, yen, Swiss, sterling. Yet gains limited before end of FOMC, key jobs report and weekend G7.

*Treasury's Rubin saying U.S. should not use dollar as trade tool helped dollar/yen, while German newpaper report U.S. eyeing strike against Iraq missile installations aided dollar/mark. Yet U.S. State Department says "no heightened concern" about Iraq.

The dollar closed firmer but gains were limited as traders awaited the conclusion of a meeting of Federal Reserve policy makers, the release of key U.S. jobs data and a weekend gathering of global financial leaders, currency experts said.
The Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) began a two-day meeting on Tuesday with any monetary policy announcement expected during Wednesday afternoon.
While most analysts saw the FOMC holding short-term interest rates steady, investors were cautious about pushing the dollar sharply higher before the results of the meeting.

"People want to be careful," said Ben Strauss, an assistant vice president of foreign exchange at Bank Julius Baer and Co. "People are willing to buy dips but not really take on a whole lot of (dollar) positions at higher levels."
The dollar ended at 1.6472/77 marks and 122.45/50 yen, up from 1.6415/20 marks and 122.10/15 yen at the open.

Investors also adopted a guarded posture ahead of the release on Friday morning of potentially market-moving United States employment figures for January and before a meeting on Saturday in Berlin of finance ministers and central bank heads of the Group of Seven leading industrial powers.

Separately, supportive comments by Treasury Secretary Robert Rubin and a German newspaper article reporting the United States was considering a missile strike against Iraq helped boost the dollar, traders said.
While speaking to reporters on Tuesday after addressing the American Association of Retired Persons, Rubin brushed aside United States automakers' complaints about the strength of the dollar.
United States automakers have repeatedly voiced concern that the sharp dollar rally against the yen is hurting their competitiveness compared with Japanese car manufacturers.
Rubin said on Tuesday the key to competitiveness is efficiency and stressed the Administration should not use the dollar as an instrument of trade policy.

"With Rubin talking about the dollar not being used as a tool of trade policy,...there was some buying of dollars for yen after that statement was made," said Doug Lee, an assistant vice president at Sakura Bank Ltd in New York.

German newspaper Frankfurter Allgemeine Zeitung reported that United Nations inspectors had discovered that Iraq has continued to develop missiles, in contravention of United Nations resolutions ending the 1991 Persian Gulf War.
The newspaper also said the United States was contemplating a possible punitive missile strike against Iraq as a result.
"That's what squeezed the market up from 1.6425 up to 1.6460 or so," said Steven Walker, a senior trader at Skandinaviska Enskilda Banken in New York, referring to the dollar's gains versus the mark.
Yet the State Department denied any such intentions, saying there was no reason for heightened concern about military action against Iraq.
Furthermore, United Nations officials and knowledgable diplomats also dismissed the newspaper report.
Elsewhere, the dollar finished at 1.4285/95 Swiss francs, up from 1.4240/50 francs at the open.
Sterling fell to $1.6195/05 from $1.6230/35.
The dollar climbed to Canadian $1.3440/45, up from C$1.3411/16.
The Australian dollar finished at $0.7633/38, unchanged from its opening level.
